commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

"""Aggregate steering results: per-condition means with bootstrap CIs, paired tests against
equal-norm random directions, matched-coherence comparison, validation of the measures.
usage: python analysis_steering.py
"""
import json, os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import wilcoxon
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from common import ROOT

S = f"{ROOT}/results/steering"
R = f"{ROOT}/results"
MEAS = ["desklib", "fakespot", "hc3rob", "bino_ai", "falcon_nll", "ai_likeness", "coherence", "relevance",
        "sim_unsteered", "sim_question", "n_words", "sent_len", "list_items", "bold", "newlines", "first_person",
        "contractions", "exclam", "ttr", "ai_phrases"]


def load(name):
    d = pd.read_json(f"{S}/{name}_scores.jsonl", lines=True)
    j = pd.read_json(f"{S}/all_judge.jsonl", lines=True).drop_duplicates("id").set_index("id")
    for k in ["ai_likeness", "coherence", "relevance"]:
        d[k] = d.uid.map(j[k]) if k in j else np.nan
    d["desklib_flag"] = (d.desklib > 0.5).astype(float)
    d["fakespot_flag"] = (d.fakespot > 0.5).astype(float)
    return d


def boot_ci(x, n=2000, seed=0):
    x = np.asarray(x, float); x = x[~np.isnan(x)]
    if len(x) == 0:
        return np.nan, np.nan
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    m = rng.choice(x, (n, len(x))).mean(1)
    return float(np.percentile(m, 2.5)), float(np.percentile(m, 97.5))


def summarize(d, name):
    rec = []
    meas = MEAS + ["desklib_flag", "fakespot_flag"]
    for (cond, fam, a), g in d.groupby(["cond", "family", "alpha"], dropna=False):
        r = dict(cond=cond, family=fam, alpha=a, n=len(g))
        for m in meas:
            if m in g and g[m].notna().any():
                r[m] = float(g[m].mean())
                lo, hi = boot_ci(g[m])
                r[m + "_lo"], r[m + "_hi"] = lo, hi
        rec.append(r)
    t = pd.DataFrame(rec)
    t.to_csv(f"{R}/steering_{name}_summary.csv", index=False)
    return t


def paired_tests(d, name, layer=12):
    """AI direction vs equal-norm random directions (mean over 3 seeds), and vs each control, per alpha."""
    rec = []
    piv = {m: d.pivot_table(index="id", columns="cond", values=m) for m in ["desklib", "fakespot", "bino_ai", "ai_likeness", "coherence", "falcon_nll"]}
    alphas = sorted(d[d.family == "ai"].alpha.unique())
    for a in alphas:
        tag = f"@L{layer}a{a:+g}"
        for m, P in piv.items():
            ai = P.get("ai" + tag)
            rnd = P[[c for c in P.columns if c.startswith("random") and c.endswith(tag)]].mean(1)
            base = P["none"]
            for other_name, other in [("random(mean of 3)", rnd), ("none", base)] + \
                    [(f, P.get(f + tag)) for f in ["ai_perp", "formality", "assistant", "fluency", "register"]]:
                if ai is None or other is None:
                    continue
                ok = ai.notna() & other.notna()
                diff = (ai[ok] - other[ok])
                p = float(wilcoxon(ai[ok], other[ok]).pvalue) if (diff != 0).any() else 1.0
                rec.append(dict(alpha=a, measure=m, vs=other_name, mean_ai=float(ai[ok].mean()),
                                mean_other=float(other[ok].mean()), diff=float(diff.mean()), p_wilcoxon=p, n=int(ok.sum())))
    t = pd.DataFrame(rec); t.to_csv(f"{R}/steering_{name}_paired_tests.csv", index=False)
    return t


def matched_coherence(t, name, tol=1.0):
    """For each steering family: the strongest strength whose mean judge coherence AND relevance stay within
    `tol` points of the unsteered baseline; report detector scores there."""
    base = t[t.cond == "none"].iloc[0]
    rec = []
    for fam, g in t.groupby("family"):
        for sign in [-1, 1]:
            gg = g[(np.sign(g.alpha) == sign)]
            ok = gg[(gg.coherence >= base.coherence - tol) & (gg.relevance >= base.relevance - tol)]
            if len(ok) == 0 and fam not in ("prompt_human", "clamp_human", "clamp_ai", "none", "ref_human", "ref_chatgpt"):
                continue
            if fam in ("prompt_human", "clamp_human", "clamp_ai", "ref_human", "ref_chatgpt", "none", "none_seed2"):
                if sign == 1:
                    continue
                ok = g
            row = ok.loc[ok.alpha.abs().idxmax()] if len(ok) else None
            if row is None:
                continue
            rec.append(dict(family=fam, alpha=row.alpha, coherence=row.coherence, relevance=row.relevance,
                            desklib=row.desklib, desklib_flag=row.desklib_flag, fakespot=row.fakespot, bino_ai=row.bino_ai,
                            ai_likeness=row.ai_likeness, falcon_nll=row.falcon_nll, sim_unsteered=row.sim_unsteered))
    m = pd.DataFrame(rec); m.to_csv(f"{R}/steering_{name}_matched_coherence.csv", index=False)
    return m


def validation():
    d = load("validation")
    rec = []
    for fam, g in d.groupby("family"):
        for gen in sorted(g.cond.unique()):
            if gen.endswith("human"):
                continue
            hum = g[g.cond.str.endswith("human")]
            ai = g[g.cond == gen]
            x = pd.concat([hum, ai]); y = (x.cond == gen).astype(int)
            r = dict(set=gen)
            for m in ["desklib", "fakespot", "hc3rob", "bino_ai", "ai_likeness", "falcon_nll"]:
                ok = x[m].notna()
                r[m] = float(roc_auc_score(y[ok], x[m][ok])) if ok.sum() > 10 else np.nan
            rec.append(r)
    v = pd.DataFrame(rec); v.to_csv(f"{R}/measure_validation_auroc.csv", index=False)
    # agreement between measures on validation + main
    return v


if __name__ == "__main__":
    out = {}
    v = validation(); print(v.round(3).to_string())
    d = load("main")
    t = summarize(d, "main")
    cols = ["cond", "desklib", "desklib_flag", "fakespot", "bino_ai", "ai_likeness", "coherence", "relevance", "falcon_nll", "sim_unsteered", "n_words", "list_items", "first_person", "contractions"]
    print(t[cols].round(3).to_string())
    pt = paired_tests(d, "main")
    mc = matched_coherence(t, "main"); print(mc.round(3).to_string())
    # correlations between measures across all main generations
    corr = d[["desklib", "fakespot", "hc3rob", "bino_ai", "ai_likeness", "coherence", "falcon_nll"]].corr(method="spearman")
    corr.to_csv(f"{R}/steering_main_measure_corr.csv")
    if os.path.exists(f"{S}/base_scores.jsonl"):
        b = load("base")
        tb = summarize(b, "base"); print(tb[cols].round(3).to_string())
        paired_tests(b, "base")

# Paper Finder

This repo contains the code for the standalone Paper Finder agent (namely PaperFinder).

This code is not actively maintained, and reflects a snapshot in time -- of the online/live PaperFinder agent -- which is easy to run locally. This is also the code that is used for evaluating PaperFinder and that can be used for reproducing the reported results.

PaperFinder is our paper-seeking agent, which is intended to assist in locating sets of papers according to content-based and metadata criteria.

### High Level Overview

PaperFinder is implemented as a pipeline of manual-coded components which involve LLM decisions in several key-points, as well as LLM-based relevance judgments of retrieved abstracts and snippets. At a high-level, a query is analyzed and transformed into a structured object which is then fed to an execution planner that routes the analyzed query to one of several workflows, each covering a particular paper-seeking intent. Each workflow may involve multiple steps, and returns a relevance-judged set of papers, which is then ranked while weighting content relevance together with other criteria which may appear in the query (e.g., "early works on", "influential" etc).

### How does this version differ from the live version?

This code departs from the PaperFinder agent which is [deployed online](https://paperfinder.allen.ai/). The online agent has several abilities that are not supported by the agent in this repo (and which are not relevant for the evaluation), such as the ability to handle multi-turn interaction with a user, to send user-friendly progress updates to a host environment, to maintain conversations over long periods of time and to show a graphical widget with the results. It also consults datasets and indices which are legal for us to use in the product but not in the public-facing API. The online agent also differs from this code in some of its configuration options, as evaluation setup differs from product setups (for example, in a product it is OK or even preferable to also show in the results papers that are ranked right after the relevant ones, to ask a user for clarifications, or to refuse some queries which seem out of scope, all of which are not advised in an evaluation setup). Finally, the online agent keeps updating regularly and is tightly integrated in the production environment. For this release we wanted a stable, consistent version, which focuses on the core capability of paper-finding given a single user query. We plan to release larger chunks of PaperFinder agent, in particular the multi-turn abilities, as they become more mature and stable, and as we have proper benchmarks for them.

This code was created by cloning the internal PaperFinder repo and brutally removing various environment, UI and conversation management related code, some internal search APIs and so on, while keeping the single-turn paper-search functionality working and effective.

## How to run

### secrets file

The agent requires multiple keys, which should be defined in a `.env.secret` file under `agents/mabool/api/conf`.
The needed keys are: `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `S2_API_KEY`, `COHERE_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`.

### Environment

We are using [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/#highlights) as our project manager, so to prepare the environement:

```bash
make sync-dev
```

### Running
To run the agent, we launch a FastAPI server. Once the server is running, we can interact with it using cURL from the command line or through the Swagger web interface.

```bash
cd agents/mabool/api
make start-dev
```

This code was created by cloning the internal PaperFinder repo and brutally removing various environment, UI and conversation management related code, some internal search APIs and so on, while keeping the single-turn paper-search functionality working and effective.

## How to run

### secrets file

The agent requires multiple keys, which should be defined in a `.env.secret` file under `agents/mabool/api/conf`.
The needed keys are: `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `S2_API_KEY`, `COHERE_API_KEY`, `GOOGLE_API_KEY`.

### Environment

We are using [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/#highlights) as our project manager, so to prepare the environement:

```bash
make sync-dev
```

### Running
To run the agent, we launch a FastAPI server. Once the server is running, we can interact with it using cURL from the command line or through the Swagger web interface.

```bash
cd agents/mabool/api
make start-dev
```

Base directory for this skill: /tmp/claude-1000/bundled-skills/2.1.283/3b75e40feaaf8563e4bb9190d69ff0a4/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

"""Figures for the paper (static PDF, matplotlib). usage: python plots.py [readout|steering|all]"""
import sys, os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from common import ROOT

R = f"{ROOT}/results"; F = f"{ROOT}/paper_draft/figures"
os.makedirs(F, exist_ok=True)
C = ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#008300", "#4a3aa7", "#e34948"]
GRAY = "#8a8a85"
plt.rcParams.update({"font.size": 8.5, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
                     "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": "#e6e6e3", "grid.linewidth": 0.6, "axes.edgecolor": "#9a9a95",
                     "lines.linewidth": 1.6, "legend.frameon": False, "figure.dpi": 200, "savefig.bbox": "tight"})
EVALS = ["HC3 (ChatGPT)", "HAP gpt-4o", "HAP llama3-8b-inst", "MAGE GPT-4 (OOD)", "MAGE chat (GPT-3.5/davinci-003)",
         "Llama-3.1 paraphrase", "HAP llama3-8b-base", "MAGE older LMs"]


def readout():
    s = pd.read_csv(f"{R}/readout_layer_sweep.csv")
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.2, 2.6), sharey=True)
    for ax, dn, title in [(axs[0], "ai", "(a) AI direction $u_{AI}$ (diff-of-means)"),
                          (axs[1], "ai_perp", "(b) $u_{AI}^{\\perp}$ (confound span removed)")]:
        for i, e in enumerate(EVALS):
            g = s[(s.model == "instruct") & (s.direction == dn) & (s["eval"] == e)].sort_values("layer")
            ax.plot(g.layer, g.auroc, color=C[i], label=e, ls="--" if ("base" in e or "older" in e) else "-")
        ax.axhline(0.5, color=GRAY, lw=0.8); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.5); ax.set_xlabel("layer")
    axs[0].set_ylabel("held-out AUROC"); axs[1].legend(fontsize=6.5, loc="lower right", ncol=1)
    fig.savefig(f"{F}/readout_layers.pdf"); plt.close(fig)

    c = pd.read_csv(f"{R}/readout_cosines.csv")
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.5, 2.5))
    for i, k in enumerate(["formality", "register", "fluency", "verbosity", "domain", "assistant"]):
        g = c[(c.model == "instruct") & (((c.a == "ai") & (c.b == k)) | ((c.b == "ai") & (c.a == k)))].sort_values("layer")
        ax.plot(g.layer, g.cos, color=C[i], label=k)
    g = c[(c.model == "instruct") & (c.a == "ai_hap") & (c.b == "ai_hc3")].sort_values("layer")
    ax.plot(g.layer, g.cos, color="black", ls=":", label="HC3 vs HAP AI dirs")
    ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8); ax.axvline(12, color=GRAY, lw=0.6, ls="--")
    ax.set_xlabel("layer"); ax.set_ylabel("cosine with $u_{AI}$"); ax.legend(fontsize=6.3, ncol=2, loc="lower left")
    fig.savefig(f"{F}/readout_cosines.pdf"); plt.close(fig)

    b = pd.read_csv(f"{R}/readout_base_vs_instruct.csv")
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.2, 2.4))
    for i, e in enumerate(["HC3 (ChatGPT)", "HAP gpt-4o", "MAGE GPT-4 (OOD)"]):
        axs[0].plot(b.layer, b[f"{e}|inst_auc"], color=C[i], label=f"{e} instruct")
        axs[0].plot(b.layer, b[f"{e}|base_auc"], color=C[i], ls="--", label=f"{e} base")

content.text:
I wrote 35 entries to `/workspaces/is-there-a-sounds-like-ai-direction-c164-zeroshot-claude-opus-5-5/paper_draft/references.bib`, and every one checked out. The web search tools weren't loaded, so I didn't use them. Instead I pulled titles, full author lists, years and IDs from the arXiv API and copied the ACL-venue details from ACL Anthology's own BibTeX. I gave a venue only where Anthology, the arXiv journal reference or DOI, or the authors' arXiv comment confirms it. Everything else is cited as an arXiv preprint.

**Keys**
- `quaremba2026linear`: linear probing for machine-generated text detection (arXiv 2608.24780; authors Quaremba, Yan, Black, Vrandecic, Simperl).
- `vishnyakov2026svdetect`: SV-Detect, detecting AI text with steering vectors (arXiv 2606.07313).
- `kuznetsov2025feature`: sparse autoencoder features for artificial text detection (Findings of ACL 2025).
- `lu2026assistant`: The Assistant Axis (arXiv 2601.10387). The full title is "...: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models"; authors Lu, Gallagher, Michala, Fish, Lindsey.
- `guo2023hc3`: the HC3 human-vs-ChatGPT comparison corpus (arXiv).
- `dugan2024raid`: the RAID detector benchmark (ACL 2024).
- `reinhart2025llms`: human-vs-LLM grammatical and rhetorical style (PNAS 2025, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2422455122).
- `li2024mage`: MAGE (ACL 2024). The current arXiv title is "MAGE: Machine-generated Text Detection in the Wild"; the earlier "Deepfake Text Detection in the Wild" name is in a note.
- `hans2024binoculars`: the Binoculars zero-shot detector (arXiv).
- `mitchell2023detectgpt`: DetectGPT (ICML 2023).
- `sadasivan2023can`: argues AI-text detection is unreliable (TMLR).
- `krishna2023paraphrasing`: paraphrasing evades detectors, retrieval defends (NeurIPS 2023).
- `turner2023steering`: activation addition steering (arXiv).
- `zou2023representation`: representation engineering (arXiv, full 21-author list).
- `li2023inference`: inference-time intervention (NeurIPS 2023).
- `arditi2024refusal`: refusal is mediated by a single direction (arXiv).
- `park2024linear`: the linear representation hypothesis (ICML 2024).
- `marks2024geometry`: The Geometry of Truth (COLM 2024).
- `rimsky2024steering`: Contrastive Activation Addition (ACL 2024). Anthology lists the first author as Rimsky; a note records the arXiv name Panickssery.
- `chen2025persona`: persona vectors (arXiv).
- `lieberum2024gemmascope`: Gemma Scope sparse autoencoders (BlackboxNLP 2024).
- `ravfogel2020null`: INLP, "Null It Out" (ACL 2020).
- `belrose2023leace`: LEACE closed-form concept erasure (arXiv).
- `qwen2025qwen25`: Qwen2.5 technical report (arXiv, December 2024). The key says 2025 but the entry's year is 2024, which is the arXiv date.
- `gemma2025gemma3`: Gemma 3 technical report (arXiv 2503.19786).
- `grattafiori2024llama3`: The Llama 3 Herd of Models (arXiv).
- `almazrouei2023falcon`: The Falcon Series of Open Language Models (arXiv).
- `reimers2019sentence`: Sentence-BERT (EMNLP 2019).
- `song2020mpnet`: MPNet (arXiv).
- `zheng2023judging`: LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks).

**Item 24 additions (5)**
- `kobak2025delving`: excess-vocabulary ("delve") evidence of LLM-assisted writing in biomedical papers (Science Advances 2025).
- `liang2024monitoring`: estimates how much of AI-conference peer-review text was modified by an LLM (ICML 2024).
- `liang2024mapping`: Liang et al. 2024 (arXiv 2404.01268), on rising LLM-modified content in scientific papers.
- `sun2025idiosyncrasies`: LLM outputs carry stylistic signatures that let a classifier tell which model wrote them (ICML 2025).
- `konen2024style`: style vectors for steering LLM output style through activations (Findings of EACL 2024).

**Not verified or caveated**
- **No item had to be omitted.**
- **Venues left off:** Binoculars, Arditi et al., LEACE, MPNet, HC3, Turner et al., Zou et al., persona vectors and Liang "Mapping" are cited as arXiv only. My unconfirmed belief is ICML 2024, NeurIPS 2024, NeurIPS 2023 and NeurIPS 2020 for the first four, and COLM 2024 for Liang "Mapping". I couldn't check these because the DBLP lookup timed out.
- **Truncated author lists:** Qwen2.5, Gemma 3 and Llama 3 list the first authors followed by "and others".
- **Rimsky key:** it uses Rimsky because that is the name on the ACL version.
- **No item-24 paper on humanizing LLM output via activation steering:** I didn't find one, so the closest verified match is Konen et al.'s style vectors.

commands.name: azure-gpu
commands.description: Request, use and release Azure GPU VMs (A100/H100/T4) for training, RL fine-tuning, vLLM serving or paper-replication jobs. Use whenever a task needs a GPU and none is attached to this machine. Wraps `az` with size allowlist, TTL tags, auto-shutdown and a reaper so nothing is left running. (user)

commands.name: deep-research
commands.description: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. (dynamic workflow)

commands.name: design
commands.description: Grant or revoke Claude agent access to your Design projects

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: schedule
commands.description: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

commands.name: workflow-authoring
commands.description: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.

commands.name: run
commands.description: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

commands.description: Author or improve the run-<unit> skill - a per-project skill that tells agents how to build, launch, and drive this project's app. Use when the user asks to set up the project, get it running, write run instructions, or verify build/run steps work from a clean environment.

commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: import-memory
commands.description: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: morning
commands.description: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: skill-creator
commands.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

"""Length-controlled detector check: re-score every main-grid text truncated to its first N words
(texts shorter than N words are dropped), so that shorter steered answers cannot look 'human' merely by length."""
import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from common import ROOT
from detectors import supervised_scores

N = 50
d = pd.read_json(f"{ROOT}/results/steering/main_scores.jsonl", lines=True)
d = d[d.n_words >= N].copy()
texts = [" ".join(t.split()[:N]) for t in d.text]
sc = supervised_scores(texts)
for k, v in sc.items():
    d[f"{k}_trunc{N}"] = v
d[["uid", "cond", "family", "alpha", f"desklib_trunc{N}", f"fakespot_trunc{N}", f"hc3rob_trunc{N}"]].to_csv(
    f"{ROOT}/results/steering_main_length_control.csv", index=False)
d["fam"] = d.family.str.replace(r"random\d", "random", regex=True)
print(d.groupby(["fam", "alpha"]).agg(n=("uid", "size"), desklib=(f"desklib_trunc{N}", "mean"), fakespot=(f"fakespot_trunc{N}", "mean")).round(3).to_string())
EOF
echo ok

             ("ai_perp@L12a-4", "$u_{AI}^{\\perp}$, $\\alpha{=}{-}4$"), ("ai_perp@L12a-6", "$u_{AI}^{\\perp}$, $\\alpha{=}{-}6$"),
             ("ai+prompt@L12a-4", "prompt + $u_{AI}$, $\\alpha{=}{-}4$"),
             ("addall_a-0.25", "$u_{AI}$ all layers, $\\alpha{=}{-}0.25$"),
             ("RANDOM-6", "random (3 seeds), $\\alpha{=}{-}6$"), ("RANDOM-8", "random (3 seeds), $\\alpha{=}{-}8$"),
             ("formality@L12a-8", "formality, $\\alpha{=}{-}8$"), ("fluency@L12a-8", "fluency, $\\alpha{=}{-}8$"),
             ("register@L12a-8", "register, $\\alpha{=}{-}8$"), ("assistant@L12a-6", "Assistant axis, $\\alpha{=}{-}6$"),
             ("clamp_human", "clamp to human mean, all layers"),
             ("ai@L12a+4", "$u_{AI}$, $\\alpha{=}{+}4$"), ("ai@L12a+8", "$u_{AI}$, $\\alpha{=}{+}8$"),
             ("ref_human", "\\emph{real human answers}"), ("ref_chatgpt", "\\emph{real ChatGPT answers}")]
    cols = ["frac_non_english", "desklib", "fakespot", "bino_ai", "desklib_logit", "coherence", "relevance", "sim_unsteered", "n_words"]
    rows = []
    for c, name in conds:
        if c.startswith("RANDOM"):
            a = c[6:]
            sub = t[t.index.str.match(rf"random\d@L12a{a}$")]
            r = sub[cols].mean(); l = lcm.loc[sub.index].mean()
        else:
            r = t.loc[c, cols]; l = lcm.loc[c] if c in lcm.index else pd.Series({"desklib_trunc50": np.nan, "fakespot_trunc50": np.nan})
        if c in ("ai@L12a-2", "ai_perp@L12a-4", "ai+prompt@L12a-4", "RANDOM-6", "clamp_human", "ai@L12a+4", "ref_human"):
            rows.append("\\midrule")
        rows.append(f"{name} & {r.frac_non_english*100:.0f} & {f3(r.desklib)} & {f3(r.fakespot)} & {f3(l.desklib_trunc50)} & {f3(l.fakespot_trunc50)} & {f3(r.bino_ai)} & {r.desklib_logit:.1f} & {r.coherence:.1f} & {r.relevance:.1f} & {f3(r.sim_unsteered)} & {r.n_words:.0f}\\\\")
    open(f"{T}/steering.tex", "w").write("\n".join(rows) + "\n")

    # matched-quality analysis: individual generations with judge coherence>=8 and relevance>=8
    d = pd.read_json(f"{R}/steering/main_scores.jsonl", lines=True)
    j = pd.read_json(f"{R}/steering/all_judge.jsonl", lines=True).drop_duplicates("id").set_index("id")
    d["coherence"] = d.uid.map(j.coherence); d["relevance"] = d.uid.map(j.relevance)
    d = d.merge(sc[["uid", "en"]], on="uid"); d = d[d.en]
    d["fam"] = d.family.str.replace(r"random\d", "random", regex=True)
    q = d[(d.coherence >= 8) & (d.relevance >= 8)]
    rows = []
    for fam, name in [("ai", "$u_{AI}$"), ("ai_perp", "$u_{AI}^{\\perp}$"), ("random", "random"), ("formality", "formality"), ("fluency", "fluency"), ("register", "register"), ("assistant", "Assistant axis")]:
        cells = []
        for a in [-4, -6, -8]:
            g = q[(q.fam == fam) & (q.alpha == a)]
            tot = len(d[(d.fam == fam) & (d.alpha == a)])
            cells.append(f"{g.desklib.mean():.2f} & {g.fakespot.mean():.2f} & {100*len(g)/max(tot,1):.0f}\\%" if len(g) else "-- & -- & 0\\%")
        rows.append(f"{name} & " + " & ".join(cells) + "\\\\")
    for c, name in [("none", "unsteered"), ("prompt_human", "prompt baseline"), ("ref_human", "real human answers")]:
        g = q[q.cond == c]; tot = len(d[d.cond == c])
        rows.append(f"{name} & \\multicolumn{{9}}{{c}}{{desklib {g.desklib.mean():.2f}, fakespot {g.fakespot.mean():.2f}, kept {100*len(g)/tot:.0f}\\%}}\\\\")
    open(f"{T}/matched_quality.tex", "w").write("\n".join(rows) + "\n")


def base():
    t = pd.read_csv(f"{R}/steering_base_summary.csv").set_index("cond")
    rows = []
    for c, name in [("none", "unsteered"), ("ai@L12a-4", "$u_{AI}^{base}$, $\\alpha{=}{-}4$"), ("ai@L12a-8", "$u_{AI}^{base}$, $\\alpha{=}{-}8$"),

    open(f"{T}/base_steering.tex", "w").write("\n".join(rows) + "\n")

A single diff-of-means direction, fit on length-matched pairs, separates held-out human and chat-model text at every layer. AUROC is 0.83--0.86 in the middle layers and up to 0.98 at layer 27. The full probe reaches 0.93--1.00. The direction transfers to generators and corpora never used for fitting: GPT-4 on MAGE (0.81 at L12, 0.91 at L27) and GPT-3.5/davinci-003 (0.74/0.88). The HC3 and HAP directions are fit on disjoint corpora (Q\&A vs.\ six prose genres) and different generators. They agree substantially (cosine 0.56 at L12; Figure~\ref{fig:cosines}), which supports a shared component across settings~\citep{quaremba2026linear}.

\textbf{What the direction does \emph{not} detect} is informative. Continuations written by Llama-3 \emph{base} models are matched to the same human prefixes as the instruct continuations. They score only 0.59--0.63, against 0.83--0.86 for Llama-3-Instruct. Text from older, pre-chat LMs (OPT, FLAN-T5, LLaMA-1, GPT-J, \dots) is at chance (0.49). Even the full probe is at chance on older LMs (0.51). It reaches 0.85--0.88 on base-model text, but that is close to what per-token NLL alone achieves (0.87--0.91). The direction therefore encodes the style of \emph{chat-tuned} models, not ``machine authorship''. That supports reading it as ``sounds like an AI assistant''.

\paragraph{Geometry.} At layer 12, $u_{AI}$ has cosine $0.68$ with formality, $0.69$ with fluency (low NLL), $0.64$ with register, $-0.58$ with verbosity and $0.40$ with the Assistant axis. Its cosine with Reddit-vs-encyclopedic domain is near zero (0.08) (Figure~\ref{fig:cosines}). Projecting $u_{AI}$ onto the 6-dimensional confound span captures 54\% of its squared norm at L12 and 25\% at L27. So the raw direction is roughly half ``formal, fluent, non-verbose, assistant-like'' text. It is clearly \emph{not} the Assistant axis, which it overlaps only moderately and less at late layers ($0.17$ at L27).

-\paragraph{The signal is not in the confounds.} Removing the whole confound span and refitting \emph{raises} held-out AUROC at L12, from 0.86--0.88 to 0.97--0.99 on matched sets and from 0.81 to 0.88 on MAGE GPT-4 (Table~\ref{tab:readout}, ``confounds''). Removing a random 6-dimensional subspace changes nothing. The confound-orthogonal direction $u_{AI}^{\perp}$ alone reads out at 0.98--0.99 on matched sets and 0.93 on MAGE GPT-4, above the best single confound direction (0.59--0.80). The confounds were mostly adding variance unrelated to authorship. Removing $u_{AI}$ itself and refitting drops AUROC to 0.34--0.71. Much of the linearly decodable signal is concentrated in this one direction, though not all of it (cf.\ INLP~\citep{ravfogel2020null}).

Removing a random 6-dimensional subspace changes nothing. The confound-orthogonal direction $u_{AI}^{\perp}$ alone reads out at 0.97--0.99 on matched sets and 0.93 on MAGE GPT-4, far above any single confound direction ($\leq 0.80$). The confounds were mostly adding variance unrelated to authorship. Removing $u_{AI}$ itself and refitting drops AUROC to 0.34--0.71. Much of the linearly decodable signal is concentrated in this one direction, though not all of it (cf.\ INLP~\citep{ravfogel2020null}).

\paragraph{Perplexity.} Perplexity is the strongest scalar confound. AI text is much more likely under Qwen (mean-NLL AUROC 0.79--0.98 on matched sets), and at L12 the raw $u_{AI}$ projection correlates with NLL ($\rho\approx-0.5$ within class). A logistic model on [NLL, length] does not improve when the $u_{AI}$ projection at L12 is added. The confound-orthogonal $u_{AI}^{\perp}$ is a different matter (Table~\ref{tab:scalar}): it adds substantial information beyond NLL and length, and it separates content-matched paraphrases, where NLL is weak (0.67). Low perplexity is part of what makes text ``sound like AI'', but it is not the whole of what the representation encodes.

\paragraph{Validity of the measures.} Before steering we checked every measure on held-out real text (Table~\ref{tab:validation}). Both supervised detectors and Binoculars separate human from AI text almost perfectly (AUROC 0.90--1.00), including base-model text. The Gemma-3-12B judge's AI-likeness rating is near chance (0.46--0.60). It also rates degenerate text as maximally AI-like (Table~\ref{tab:steer_full} in the appendix). We therefore do \textbf{not} use the judge for AI-ness. We keep it only for coherence and relevance, for which it behaves sensibly (unsteered 9.1/9.4; real human answers 8.1/8.5; broken text 1.0). This agrees with the warning in the task framing that LLM judges are noisy on ``sounds like AI''.

The unsteered model is detected as AI on essentially every answer (desklib 0.99, fakespot 0.99). Subtracting $u_{AI}$ lowers both supervised detectors and Binoculars, monotonically in $|\alpha|$. At $\alpha{=}{-}6$, mean P(AI) is 0.42 (desklib) and 0.34 (fakespot), and Binoculars moves most of the way from the model ($-0.69$) to real human answers ($-0.99$). The real human answers to the same questions score 0.34/0.23/$-0.99$. So did the formality, register and fluency directions (0.95--0.99 at $\alpha{=}{-}8$) and the Assistant axis (0.72--0.83), even though each of them shares 0.4--0.7 cosine with $u_{AI}$.

In logit space it still pushes beyond the unsteered model (desklib logit 8.8 $\rightarrow$ 11.7 at $\alpha{=}{+}8$; random 9.8, formality 9.9). \paragraph{Coherence cost and matched-quality comparison.} The effect costs some quality. At $\alpha{=}{-}4$ judge coherence falls only from 9.1 to 8.9, and relevance even rises (9.6), but the detectors only reach 0.83/0.87. At $\alpha{=}{-}6$ coherence is 6.8 (real human answers: 8.1). Two observations show the detector shift is not a by-product of degradation. First, equal-norm random directions at $\alpha{=}{-}8$ degrade coherence comparably (7.6--8.7) without moving the detectors. Second, Table~\ref{tab:matched} keeps only answers the judge rates $\geq 8$ on \emph{both} coherence and relevance. Among these high-quality answers, $u_{AI}$ at $\alpha{=}{-}6$ still scores 0.53/0.42 and $u_{AI}^{\perp}$ scores 0.40/0.30, which matches real human answers that pass the same filter (0.36/0.26). -\paragraph{The confound-orthogonal component is the better steering vector.} $u_{AI}^{\perp}$ has no component along formality, register, fluency, verbosity, domain or the Assistant axis. The causal effect on detectors therefore does not run through the measured confounds.

# Is there a "sounds like AI" direction in the residual stream?

Paper: [`paper_draft/main.pdf`](paper_draft/main.pdf) (LaTeX source in `paper_draft/`).

## Question
Human vs. AI text is known to be linearly separable in LLM activations. We ask:
1. **Causal?** Does adding or subtracting the human-vs-AI direction during generation make the model's *own* output read as more or less AI-written to *independent* detectors, while keeping coherence and content?
2. **Distinct?** Is it an "AI-ness" direction, or a relabelling of formality, fluency (perplexity), register, domain, verbosity or the Assistant persona?
3. **Base vs. instruct?** Does it exist in the pretrained base model, and does chat tuning amplify it?

## What we did
* **Model:** Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B (base). Residual stream mean-pooled over ≤128 tokens of raw text. Every matched group (same question / same prefix) is cut to the same token length.
* **Data:** HC3 (question-matched human vs ChatGPT; PTB artefacts detokenised on both sides), the human-AI parallel corpus (prefix-matched human vs GPT-4o / GPT-4o-mini / Llama-3-Instruct / Llama-3 base), MAGE (OOD, 30+ generators) and MAGE-GPT4. Also 500 human passages rewritten by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in formal, informal and paraphrase versions.
* **Directions:** diff-of-means `u_AI` (HC3 + HAP pooled), plus six authorship-controlled confound directions: formality, register, domain, fluency, verbosity, and the Assistant axis (default Assistant vs. 24 role-play personas). `u_AI⊥` is `u_AI` with the confound span projected out.
* **Steering:** activation addition at layer 12 with strength in units of the human–AI gap, on 160 held-out HC3 questions. Equal-norm controls: 3 random directions, the confound directions, `u_AI⊥`, a "write like a human" system prompt, prompt+steer, multi-layer addition and clamping. Also steering of the base model on 160 human text prefixes.
* **Independent measures** (none sees Qwen activations): desklib and fakespot supervised detectors, Binoculars (Falcon-7B/-Instruct), a Gemma-3-12B judge (coherence/relevance), Falcon NLL, mpnet similarity to the unsteered answer, and stylometrics. All are validated on real held-out human/AI text.

## Main findings
* **Read-out:** `u_AI` gives AUROC 0.83–0.86 (mid layers) and up to 0.98 (L27) on held-out matched sets. It transfers to MAGE GPT-4 and to content-matched paraphrases. It does **not** detect base-model or pre-chat LM text (0.49–0.63), so it encodes **chat-assistant style**, not machine authorship.
* **Disentanglement:** about 54% of `u_AI`'s squared norm (L12) lies in the confound span (cos ≈0.68 formality, 0.69 fluency, 0.40 Assistant axis). Removing that span makes the read-out **better** (0.97–0.99), and `u_AI⊥` alone reads out at 0.97–0.99.
* **Causal:** subtracting `u_AI` at L12 lowers P(AI) from 0.99 to 0.42/0.34 (desklib/fakespot, α=−6). Binoculars moves to the human level, and the effect survives length control. Equal-norm random, formality, fluency and register directions stay at 0.95–1.00; the Assistant axis reaches 0.72 (α=−6) at a large coherence cost. The "write like a human" prompt leaves 99% flagged. Among answers the judge rates ≥8 on both coherence and relevance, `u_AI⊥` at α=−6 gives 0.40/0.30, matching real human answers (0.36/0.26). Adding the direction produces stock assistant prose.
* **Base vs. instruct:** base and instruct directions have cosine ≥0.98 at every layer with equal read-out AUROC, so chat tuning did not create or amplify the direction. Steering the base model with its own direction works in both directions.
* **Caveats:** the strongest settings cost coherence and sometimes switch the output to Chinese (excluded from the primary analysis). Clamping or ablating at all layers breaks the model. The LLM judge **cannot** tell human from AI text (AUROC ≤0.60), so AI-ness claims rest on the detectors and Binoculars.

## Layout
```
src/
  prepare_data.py      corpora -> data/processed/*.jsonl
  make_rewrites.py     formal/informal/paraphrase rewrites (Llama-3.1-8B via vLLM)
  extract_acts.py      mean-pooled residual activations, all layers (instruct|base)
  assistant_axis.py    persona generations + Assistant axis
  directions.py        all directions per layer (incl. u_AI_perp, projection stats)
  analysis_readout.py  layer sweep, probes, cosines, nullspace test, NLL/length controls, base vs instruct
  steer.py, run_steering.py   steering hooks; pilot / main grid / base-model experiment
  detectors.py, eval_steering.py, judge.py, vllm_chat.py   independent measures
  make_validation.py   real-text validation set for the measures
  length_control.py    detectors on first-50-word truncations
  analysis_steering.py summaries with bootstrap CIs, paired Wilcoxon tests, matched coherence
  make_tables.py, plots.py    LaTeX tables and figures for the paper
  pipeline2.sh         base steering -> detection -> judge
results/               CSV summaries; results/steering/*.jsonl = every generation with all scores
paper_draft/           main.tex, sections/, tables/ (generated), figures/ (generated), references.bib
logs/                  run logs
```
`data/`, `hf_cache/`, `.venv*/` and `bin/` hold large or local files and are git-ignored.

## Reproduce
```bash
uv venv .venv -p 3.12 && uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python torch==2.8.0 transformers==4.56.2 "sentence-transformers<5.2" accelerate datasets scikit-learn pandas matplotlib scipy pymupdf
uv venv .venv-vllm -p 3.12 && uv pip install --python .venv-vllm/bin/python vllm ziglang   # judge / rewrites
# no system C compiler here: bin/cc wraps `python -m ziglang cc` for Triton (export CC=$PWD/bin/cc), and VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0
export HF_HOME=$PWD/hf_cache   # needs HF_TOKEN with access to gemma-3 / Llama-3.1
cd src
python prepare_data.py
python make_rewrites.py prep && ../.venv-vllm/bin/python vllm_chat.py meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ../data/processed/rewrite_requests.jsonl ../data/processed/rewrite_outputs.jsonl 0.7 400 && python make_rewrites.py collect
for m in instruct base; do python extract_acts.py $m; python assistant_axis.py $m; python directions.py $m; done
python analysis_readout.py
python run_steering.py pilot && python eval_steering.py detect pilot
python run_steering.py main 12 -8,-6,-4,-2,2,4,6,8
python make_validation.py && ./pipeline2.sh
python length_control.py && python analysis_steering.py && python make_tables.py && python plots.py all
cd ../paper_draft && latexmk -pdf main.tex
```
Hardware used: 1× RTX A6000 (48 GB). The full pipeline takes about 4 GPU-hours.

All are validated on real held-out human/AI text.

+* **Read-out:** `u_AI` gives AUROC 0.83–0.86 (mid layers) and up to 0.98 (L27) on held-out matched sets. It transfers to MAGE GPT-4 and to content-matched paraphrases. It does **not** detect base-model or pre-chat LM text (0.49–0.63), so it encodes **chat-assistant style**, not machine authorship.

+* **Disentanglement:** about 54% of `u_AI`'s squared norm (L12) lies in the confound span (cos ≈0.68 formality, 0.69 fluency, 0.40 Assistant axis). Removing that span makes the read-out **better** (0.97–0.99), and `u_AI⊥` alone reads out at 0.97–0.99.

+* **Causal:** subtracting `u_AI` at L12 lowers P(AI) from 0.99 to 0.42/0.34 (desklib/fakespot, α=−6). Binoculars moves to the human level, and the effect survives length control. Equal-norm random, formality, fluency and register directions stay at 0.95–1.00; the Assistant axis reaches 0.72 (α=−6) at a large coherence cost. The "write like a human" prompt leaves 99% flagged. Among answers the judge rates ≥8 on both coherence and relevance, `u_AI⊥` at α=−6 gives 0.40/0.30, matching real human answers (0.36/0.26). Adding the direction produces stock assistant prose.

+* **Base vs. instruct:** base and instruct directions have cosine ≥0.98 at every layer with equal read-out AUROC, so chat tuning did not create or amplify the direction. Steering the base model with its own direction works in both directions.

+* **Caveats:** the strongest settings cost coherence and sometimes switch the output to Chinese (excluded from the primary analysis). Clamping or ablating at all layers breaks the model. The LLM judge **cannot** tell human from AI text (AUROC ≤0.60), so AI-ness claims rest on the detectors and Binoculars.

\item \textbf{Read-out, with length and content control.} A diff-of-means ``AI direction'' fit on question-matched (HC3) and prefix-matched (human-AI parallel corpus) pairs, with every pair cut to the same token length, transfers to held-out generators (GPT-4o, Llama-3-Instruct, GPT-4 on MAGE) and to content-matched paraphrases. It does \emph{not} detect text from base (non-chat) LMs or older pre-chat generators (AUROC $\approx$0.5--0.65). So it encodes chat-model style, not machine authorship as such.

-    \item \textbf{Disentanglement.} The raw direction is about half confound: $\sim$54\% of its squared norm at layer 12 lies in the span of six confound directions (formality, register, domain, fluency, verbosity, Assistant axis), and it has cosine 0.6--0.7 with formality and fluency but only 0.3--0.4 with the Assistant axis. Projecting that span out does \emph{not} remove the signal. The remaining confound-orthogonal component $u_{AI}^{\perp}$ is a \emph{better} detector (AUROC 0.97--0.99 vs.\ 0.86--0.88).

-    \item \textbf{Causality.} Subtracting the direction at one middle layer makes the instruct model's answers read as human to two independent supervised detectors, a zero-shot detector (Binoculars) and an LLM judge. Matched-norm random directions do nothing, and confound directions do less. We characterise the coherence cost and compare with a ``write like a human'' prompt at matched coherence (\S\ref{sec:steer}).

content.text:
I've finished the project: the paper is at `paper_draft/main.pdf` (17 pages, compiled from `paper_draft/main.tex`) and the `README.md` covers the question, method, findings and how to rerun it. All experiments ran on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and its base model. Every number in the paper comes from scripts in `src/`, and every generation with all its scores is in `results/`.

**Findings**
1. **Read-out.** A single "AI direction" (the mean difference between human and AI text) separates held-out human from chat-model text. Within a pair, human and AI texts were cut to the same number of tokens. AUROC is 0.83–0.86 at the middle layers and up to 0.98 at layer 27. It transfers to GPT-4 text from another dataset and to paraphrases where only the author changes. It does **not** detect text from base models or older pre-chat generators (AUROC 0.49–0.63). So it captures chat-assistant style, not "written by a machine" in general.
2. **Disentanglement.**
   - About 54% of the direction lies in the span of six confound directions, each built with authorship held fixed: formality, register, domain, perplexity, verbosity and the Assistant persona axis.
   - Its cosine with formality and with perplexity is about 0.7; with the Assistant axis it is 0.40.
   - Removing that span makes it a *better* detector (AUROC 0.97–0.99). The raw direction at layer 12 is largely a perplexity signal, but the confound-free part adds real information beyond perplexity and length.
3. **Causal effect.** Subtracting the direction at layer 12 while the model answers 160 held-out questions:
   - Two independent detectors drop from P(AI) 0.99 to 0.42 (desklib) and 0.34 (fakespot). The zero-shot detector Binoculars moves to the level of real human answers.
   - The effect survives scoring only the first 50 words, and survives restricting to answers rated coherent and relevant. There, the confound-free direction scores 0.40/0.30 against 0.36/0.26 for real human answers.
   - Controls of the same size barely move the detectors: random directions stay at 0.98–1.00, formality/register/perplexity at 0.95–0.96, and the Assistant axis reaches 0.72 only by wrecking coherence.
   - A "write like a human" prompt leaves 99% of answers flagged.
   - Adding the direction produces stock assistant prose, in both the chat and base models.
4. **Base vs. instruct.** The direction in the base model is nearly identical to the instruct one (cosine ≥0.98 at every layer) and reads out equally well. Chat tuning did not create or amplify it.

**Problems I hit, all reported in the paper**
- **API access.** OpenRouter had no credits and the OpenAI key was rejected. I ran the judge (Gemma-3-12B) and the formality rewrites (Llama-3.1-8B) locally instead.

**Findings**
1. **Read-out.** A single "AI direction" (the mean difference between human and AI text) separates held-out human from chat-model text. Within a pair, human and AI texts were cut to the same number of tokens. AUROC is 0.83–0.86 at the middle layers and up to 0.98 at layer 27. It transfers to GPT-4 text from another dataset and to paraphrases where only the author changes. It does **not** detect text from base models or older pre-chat generators (AUROC 0.49–0.63). So it captures chat-assistant style, not "written by a machine" in general.
2. **Disentanglement.**
   - About 54% of the direction lies in the span of six confound directions, each built with authorship held fixed: formality, register, domain, perplexity, verbosity and the Assistant persona axis.
   - Its cosine with formality and with perplexity is about 0.7; with the Assistant axis it is 0.40.
   - Removing that span makes it a *better* detector (AUROC 0.97–0.99). The raw direction at layer 12 is largely a perplexity signal, but the confound-free part adds real information beyond perplexity and length.
3. **Causal effect.** Subtracting the direction at layer 12 while the model answers 160 held-out questions:
   - Two independent detectors drop from P(AI) 0.99 to 0.42 (desklib) and 0.34 (fakespot). The zero-shot detector Binoculars moves to the level of real human answers.
   - The effect survives scoring only the first 50 words, and survives restricting to answers rated coherent and relevant. There, the confound-free direction scores 0.40/0.30 against 0.36/0.26 for real human answers.
   - Controls of the same size barely move the detectors: random directions stay at 0.98–1.00, formality/register/perplexity at 0.95–0.96, and the Assistant axis reaches 0.72 only by wrecking coherence.
   - A "write like a human" prompt leaves 99% of answers flagged.
   - Adding the direction produces stock assistant prose, in both the chat and base models.
4. **Base vs. instruct.** The direction in the base model is nearly identical to the instruct one (cosine ≥0.98 at every layer) and reads out equally well. Chat tuning did not create or amplify it.
